title: Jeeno Thitikul, seeking first career major, jumps out to lead at AIG Women’s Open
content:
LYTHAM ST ANNES, England — World No. 2 Jeeno Thitikul got off to the perfect start at the AIG Women’s Open at Royal Lytham & St Annes with a bogey-free round of 64 on Thursday.

The 23-year-old from Thailand had seven birdies to claim a two-shot lead going into the second round on the west Lancashire coast as she seeks her first major win.

After becoming the youngest player to win a professional tournament with her victory at the Thailand Championship on the Ladies European Tour as a 14-year-old amateur, Thitikul has long been tipped to become a major champion, but that crown has eluded her.

She has settled for six top-10 finishes at majors and came agonisingly close to winning the Amundi Evian Championship in 2025, losing in a playoff to Grace Kim.

Thitikul’s 7-under-par round here is a strong start and puts her ahead of two-time major winner Haeran Ryu and Japanese golfer Shiho Kuwaki.

“When I always step up in the major week, I’m not really expecting to like win-win it, win like a trophy, because like it’s just really out of my control,” Thitikul said. “What I can control is if I am beating the course every day, I should have a really good chance to be on the leaderboard. If you can put a red number on your scorecard every day, which means you beat the course — and the golf course in a major week isn’t that easy to be beating.”

Ryu’s incredible run is showing no signs of slowing down as she shot 5 under par on Thursday. The 25-year-old is aiming to become the first player to win three women’s majors in a row since South Korean compatriot Inbee Park, a seven-time major champion, achieved the feat back in 2013.

What would make a win this week even more remarkable is that this is Ryu’s third tournament start since minor surgery earlier in the year, which forced her to take six weeks off and miss the U.S. Women’s Open.

Her return came at the KPMG Women’s PGA Championship at Hazeltine National Golf Club, where she emerged from a crowded leaderboard to claim her first major title.

Ryu, who has vaulted all the way to No. 3 in the world, then had to wait just 14 days for her second major trophy at the Amundi Evian Championship in France. Propelled by a record-breaking Saturday round of 60, the lowest in major tournament history, Ryu remained steady to win a nervy playoff hole against Canadian Brooke Henderson.

Since winning her first major, Ryu has said the pressure is off, which is helping her play her best golf. This is why she is not thinking too much about Sunday and what it would feel like to win a third major in a row.

“Today’s score is pretty good, but we have three more days, and this is a major,” Ryu said. “So, I just keep thinking about myself, no win (not about winning) and keep enjoying the golf course.”

Kuwaki said her putt from six meters out early in her round got her into the right rhythm to tackle a course which has an alarming amount of bunkers — 166 to be precise. Golfers must also battle typically difficult winds, synonymous with links courses like Royal Lytham & St Annes, which will host the men’s Open Championship in two years.

“I managed my game well despite the strong winds, and I was able to hole some key putts. I stayed focused throughout the round and finished with such a good score,” Kuwaki said. “It should be windy again tomorrow, so I will make sure to manage my game well and stay patient when I need to.”

American Yealimi Noh was the initial clubhouse leader with a 4-under-par round. Noh, who is tied for fourth alongside Frenchwoman Celine Boutier, missed the cut at the previous two majors but said some recent time out has helped her come back to golf feeling mentally refreshed.

“I’ve been really grinding over the last few months and not seeing the results that I wanted,” Noh said. “And then just getting really stressed over the ball and at the golf course. So just going back home the last few weeks and just coming here with a fresh start. I’m really happy to put a solid round in today.”
